newsitem.title: PERU: Japan backs Peru's tough stand in hostage deadlock.
newsitem.headline: Japan backs Peru's tough stand in hostage deadlock.

text.p: Peru's government and rebels remained deadlocked on Monday on the 34th day of the hostage crisis at the Japanese embassy residence as Japan's Prime Minister vowed not to give in to "terrorism."

Reinforcing Peru's unflinching stand against Marxist rebels holding 73 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto told Japan's parliament in Tokyo "Japan will never give in to terrorism."

"Terrorist activity is a grave challenge to all states and societies and it is vital for the international community to tackle terrorism in unity," Hashimoto said. He reiterated his "complete confidence" in Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori's hardline stand refusing to consider the rebels' main demand for the release of about 400 jailed comrades.

Both sides in Peru insist they are ready to talk but a face-to-face meeting remains on hold because the goverment rules out considering rebel releases, which the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) insists be discussed.

With the government and rebels stuck in uncompromising positions, a Japanese task force in Lima stepped up efforts to ease the ordeal for the hostages including Japanese diplomats and businessmen who have been held since Dec. 17.

The Japanese officials arranged to play soothing tunes to the hostages via a local radio station. The songs, two Japanese and one Spanish, were intended to have a relaxing effect and cheer the captives, a task force spokesman said.
He said the station would also play "radio gymnastics" -- tunes to which listeners perform stretching exercises popular in Japan.

There was minimal activity at the residence on Monday morning. Journalists ousted by police from close-up positions in a tightening of security over the weekend took up new vantage points from nearby apartments and rooftops.

One rebel briefly showed his face at a window of the residence and hostages were seen at windows hanging clothes out to dry. The captives heard Mass on Sunday from Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, the Vatican's representative and a close friend of Fujimori who is due to sit on a negotiating commission.

The VIP hostages also received counselling from a captive Jesuit priest who has rejected a chance at freedom to help the others, who include Peruvian government and security force officials, two ambassadors, and Fujimori's younger brother Pedro as well as the Japanese businessmen and diplomats.

The rebels have started to use their captives as workhands. One of the hostages spent nearly an hour at the front of the compound on Sunday taking batteries from cars parked outside the building into the home.
The hostage, identified by witnesses as Japanese Embassy official Akihisa Ouyigama, removed batteries from two vehicles, which the rebels apparently want to use in radios.
Peruvian daily Expreso reported on Monday that MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini was communicating with fellow rebels throughout Peru via coded radio messages.

"The messages that are being sent from the radio, according to the police, are camouflaged through a system of binary numbers whose content is only know by Cerpa and the comrades backing him up from outside the residence," Expreso said, adding that the code system was changed every week.
